body.input: If we don't protect the rights and the liberties

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: of those whom the society deems to be the least

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: and the last, the unpopular client,

body.input: of a client like Harvey Weinstein,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: in which the state will respect the civil rights

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: and civil liberties of people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: And these are the sorts of cases that test it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: So, for example, there was a young man many, many years ago

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: named Ernesto Miranda.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: By all accounts, he was not a likable guy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: He was a three time knife thief and not a likable guy,

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: that officers are forced to give to people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: So it is through these cases that we express oftentimes

metadata.title: Podcast: Ronald Sullivan: The Ideal of Justice in the Face of Controversy and Evil | Lex Fridman Podcast #170

body.input: the best values in our criminal justice system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So we couldn't. So this is much like an exhibit, like for a musician or a boxer or something like

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: that. Nevertheless, you were keeping track of the money and brought us one close to $2 million

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: I think. So if it was for real money, if you were able to earn money, that was a quite impressive

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: and inspiring achievement. Just a few details. What were the players looking at? Were they behind

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: a computer? What was the interface like? Yes, they were playing much like they normally do.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: These top players, when they play this game, they play mostly online. So they're used to playing

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: through a UI. And they did the same thing here. So there was this layout. You could imagine

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: there's a table on the screen. There's the human sitting there. And then there's the AI sitting

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: there. And the screen shows everything that's happening. The cards coming out and shows the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: bets being made. And we also had the betting history for the human. So if the human forgot

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: what had happened in the hand so far, they could actually reference back and so forth.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Is there a reason they were given access to the betting history for?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Well, it didn't really matter. They wouldn't have forgotten anyway. These are top quality people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: But we just wanted to put out there so it's not a question of the human forgetting and the AI

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: somehow trying to get advantage of better memory. So what was that like? I mean, that was an

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: incredible accomplishment. So what did it feel like before the event? Did you have doubt, hope?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Or where was your confidence at? Yeah, that's great. Great question. So 18

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: months earlier, I had organized a similar brains versus AI competition with our previous AI called

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Cloudico. And we couldn't beat the humans. So this time around, it was only 18 months later.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And I knew that this new AI, Libratus, was way stronger. But it's hard to say how you'll do

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: against the top humans before you try. So I thought we had about a 50-50 shot. And the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: international betting sites put us as a four to one or five to one underdog. So it's kind of

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: interesting that people really believe in people and over AI. People don't just over believe in

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: themselves, but they have overconfidence in other people as well compared to the performance of AI.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And yeah, so we were a four to one or five to one underdog. And even after three days of beating the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: humans in a row, we were still 50-50 on the international betting sites. Do you think there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: something special and magical about poker and the way people think about it? In a sense, you have,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: I mean, even in chess, there's no Hollywood movies. Poker is the star of many movies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And there's this feeling that certain human facial expressions and body language, eye movement,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: all these tells are critical to poker. Like you can look into somebody's soul and understand

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: their betting strategy and so on. So that's probably why, possibly, do you think that is why

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: people have a confidence that humans will outperform, because AI systems cannot, in this

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: construct, perceive these kinds of tells. They're only looking at betting patterns and

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: nothing else, the betting patterns and statistics. So what's more important to you if you step back

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: on human players, human versus human, what's the role of these tells, of these ideas that we

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: romanticize? Yeah. So I'll split it into two parts. So one is why do humans trust humans more than AI

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: and have overconfidence in humans? I think that's not really related to the tell question. It's just

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: that they've seen these top players, how good they are, and they're really fantastic. So it's just

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: hard to believe that an AI could beat them. So I think that's where that comes from. And that's

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: actually maybe a more general lesson about AI, that until you've seen it overperform a human,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: it's hard to believe that it could. But then the tells, a lot of these top players, they're so good

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: at hiding tells that among the top players, it's actually not really worth it for them to invest a

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: lot of effort trying to find tells in each other, because they're so good at hiding them. So yes,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: at the kind of Friday evening game, tells are going to be a huge thing. You can read other

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: people and if you're a good reader, you'll read them like an open book. But at the top levels of

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: poker now, the tells become a much smaller and smaller aspect of the game as you go to the top

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: levels. The amount of strategies, the amounts of possible actions is very large, 10 to the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: power of 100 plus. So there has to be some, I've read a few of the papers related,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: it has to form some abstractions of various hands and actions. So what kind of abstractions

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: are effective for the game of poker? Yeah, so you're exactly right. So when you go from a game tree,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: that's 10 to the 161, especially in an imperfect information game, it's way too large to solve

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: directly, even with our fastest equilibrium finding algorithms. So you want to abstract it first.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And abstraction in games is much trickier than abstraction in MDPs or other single agent settings,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: because you have these abstraction pathologies that if I have a finer grained abstraction,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: the strategy that I can get from that for the real game might actually be worse than the strategy

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: I can get from the coarse grained abstraction. So you have to be very careful. Now the kinds of

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: abstractions just to zoom out, we're talking about there's the hands abstractions and then there's

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: betting strategies. Yeah, betting actions. Yeah, so there's information abstraction,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: talk about general games, information abstraction, which is the abstraction of what chance does. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: this would be the cards in the case of poker. And then there's action abstraction, which is

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: abstracting the actions of the actual players, which would be bets in the case of poker.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Yourself and the other players? Yes, yourself and other players. And

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: for information abstraction, we were completely automated. So these were, these are algorithms,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: but they do what we call potential aware abstraction, where we don't just look at the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: value of the hand, but also how it might materialize in the good or bad hands over time. And it's

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: a certain kind of bottom up process with integer programming there and clustering and various

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: aspects, how do you build this abstraction? And then in the action abstraction there,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: it's largely based on how humans and other AI's have played this game in the past. But in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: beginning, we actually use an automated action abstraction technology, which is provably convergent

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: and that it finds the optimal combination of bet sizes, but it's not very scalable. So we

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: couldn't use it for the whole game, but we used it for the first couple of betting actions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So what's more important, the strength of the hand, so the information abstraction or the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: how you play them, the actions, does it, you know, the romanticized notion again is that it doesn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: matter what hands you have, that the actions, the betting may be the way you win no matter what

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: hands you have. Yeah. So that's why you have to play a lot of hands so that the role of luck

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: gets smaller. So you could otherwise get lucky and get some good hands and then you're going

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: to win the match. Even with thousands of hands, you can get lucky because there's so much variance in

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: No Limit Texas Hold'em because if we both go all in, it's a huge stack of variance. So there are

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: these massive swings in No Limit Texas Hold'em. So that's why you have to play not just thousands,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: but over a hundred thousand hands to get statistical significance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So let me ask another way this question. If you didn't even look at your hands,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: but they didn't know that, your opponents didn't know that, how well would you be able to do?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: That's a good question. There's actually, I heard this story that there's this Norwegian female

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: poker player called Annette Oberstad who's actually won a tournament by doing exactly that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: but that would be extremely rare. So you cannot really play well that way.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So the hands do have some role to play. Yes. So Lebradis does not use,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: as far as I understand, use learning methods, deep learning. Is there room for learning?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: There's no reason why Lebradis doesn't combine with an AlphaGo type approach for estimating the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: quality for a function estimator. What are your thoughts on this, maybe as compared to

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: another algorithm, which I'm not that familiar with, DeepStack, the engine that does use deep

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: learning that is unclear how well it does, but nevertheless uses deep learning. So what are

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: your thoughts about learning methods to aid in the way that Lebradis plays?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: In the way that Lebradis plays the game of poker.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Yeah. So as you said, Lebradis did not use learning methods and played very well without them. Since

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: then we have actually, actually here, we have a couple of papers on things that do use learning

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: techniques and deep learning in particular. And sort of the way you're talking about where

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: it's learning an evaluation function. But in imperfect information games, unlike, let's say

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: in Go, or now also in chess and shogi, it's not sufficient to learn an evaluation for a state

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: because the value of an information set depends not only on the exact state, but it also depends on

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: both players' beliefs. Like if I have a bad hand, I'm much better off if the opponent thinks I have

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: a good hand and vice versa. If I have a good hand, I'm much better off if the opponent believes I

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: have a bad hand. So the value of a state is not just a function of the cards. It depends on,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: if you will, the path of play, but only to the extent that is captured in the belief distributions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So that's why it's not as simple as it is in perfect information games. And I don't want to

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: say it's simple there either. It's of course very complicated computationally there too,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: but at least conceptually it's very straightforward. There's a state,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: there's an evaluation function. You can try to learn it. Here you have to do something more.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And what we do is in one of these papers, we're looking at allowing, where we allow the opponent

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: to actually take different strategies at the leaf of the search tree, if you will. And that

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: is a different way of doing it. And it doesn't assume there for a particular way that the opponent

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: plays, but it allows the opponent to choose from a set of different continuation strategies.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And that forces us to not be too optimistic in our lookahead search. And that's one way you can do

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: sound lookahead search in imperfect information games, which is very difficult. And you were

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: asking about DeepStack. What they did, it was very different than what we do, either in Libratus or

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: in this new work. They were randomly generating various situations in the game. Then they were

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: doing the lookahead from there to the end of the game, as if that was the start of a different game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And then they were using deep learning to learn those values of those states. But the states were

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: not just the physical states. They include the belief distributions. When you talk about lookahead

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: for DeepStack or with Libratus, does it mean considering every possibility that the game

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: can evolve? Are we talking about extremely sort of this exponentially growth of a tree?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Yes. So we're talking about exactly that. Much like you do in alpha beta search or

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Monte Carlo tree search, but with different techniques. So there's a different search

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: algorithm. And then we have to deal with the leaves differently. So if you think about what

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Libratus did, we didn't have to worry about this because we only did it at the end of the game.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So we would always terminate into a real situation and we would know what the payout is. It didn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: do these depth limited lookaheads. But now in this new paper, which is called depth limited,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: I think it's called depth limited search for imperfect information games, we can actually do

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: sound depth limited lookaheads. So we can actually start to do the lookahead from the beginning of

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: the game on because that's too complicated to do for this whole long game. So in Libratus,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: we were just doing it for the end. So, and then the other side, this belief

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: distribution. So is it explicitly modeled what kind of beliefs that the opponent might have?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Yeah, yeah, it is explicitly modeled, but it's not assumed. The beliefs are actually output,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: not input. Of course, the starting beliefs are input, but they just fall from the rules of the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: game because we know that the dealer deals uniformly from the deck. So I know that every

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: pair of cards that you might have is equally likely. I know that for a fact, that just follows from

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: the rules of the game. Of course, except the two cards that I have, I know you don't have those.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: You have to take that into account. That's called card removal and that's very important.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Is the dealing always coming from a single deck in heads up? So you can assume...

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Single deck. So you know that if I have the ace of spades, I know you don't have an ace of spades.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Great. So in the beginning, your belief is basically the fact that it's a fair

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: dealing of hands, but how do you start to adjust that belief?

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Well, that's where this beauty of game theory comes. So Nash equilibrium, which John Nash

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: introduced in 1950, introduces what rational play is when you have more than one player.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And these are pairs of strategies where strategies are contingency plans, one for each player.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So that neither player wants to deviate to a different strategy, given that the other

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: doesn't deviate. But as a side effect, you get the beliefs from base rule. So Nash equilibrium

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: really isn't just deriving in these imperfect information games. Nash equilibrium doesn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: just define strategies. It also defines beliefs for both of us and defines beliefs for each state.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So at each state, each, if they're called information sets, at each information set in the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: game, there's a set of different states that we might be in, but I don't know which one we're in.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Nash equilibrium tells me exactly what is the probability distribution over those

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: not being explainable. Game theoretic methods, you know, Nash equilibria, do they generally,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: when you see the different solutions, are they, when you talk about military operations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: are they, once you see the strategies, do they make sense? Are they explainable or do they suffer

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: from the same problems as neural networks do? So that's a good question. I would say a little

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: bit yes and no. And what I mean by that is that these game theoretic strategies, let's say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Nash equilibrium, it has provable properties. So it's unlike, let's say, deep learning where

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: you kind of cross your fingers, hopefully it'll work. And then after the fact, when you have the

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: weights, you're still crossing your fingers and I hope it will work. Here, you know that

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: the solution quality is there, this provable solution quality guarantees. Now, that doesn't

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: necessarily mean that the strategies are human understandable. That's a whole other problem. So

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: I think that deep learning and computational game theory are in the same boat in that sense,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: that both are difficult to understand. But at least the game theoretic techniques, they have these

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: guarantees of solution quality. So do you see business operations, strategic operations,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: even military in the future being at least the strong candidates being proposed by automated

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: systems? Do you see that? Yeah, I do. I do. But that's more of a belief than a substantiated fact.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Depending on where you land in optimism or pessimism, that's a really, to me, that's an

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: in my own work, what we've done so far, we run the nationwide kidney exchange. Hundreds of people

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: exchange. You have extra surgeons, nurses, anesthesiologists, hospitals, all of that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: So employment is increasing from that and the world is becoming a better place. Another example is

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: combinatorial sourcing auctions. We did 800 large scale combinatorial sourcing auctions from 2001

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: in the world. And this is not like shifting value from somebody to somebody else,

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: to stay in it for a little longer because I think game theory has a role to play here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: Let me actually come back on that as one thing. I think AI is also going to make the world

body.input: same as human civilization, human beings. So it seems like game theory has a role to play there

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: world safer? Yeah, I think this value misalignment is a fairly theoretical worry. And I haven't really

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: seen it in it because I do a lot of real applications. I don't see it anywhere. The

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: closest I've seen it was the following type of mental exercise, really, where I had this argument

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: in the late 80s when we were building these transportation optimization systems. And somebody

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: had heard that it's a good idea to have high utilization of assets. So they told me, hey, why

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: phenomenon. I've known this for over 30 years, but I've never seen it actually be a problem in reality.

metadata.title: Podcast: Tuomas Sandholm: Poker and Game Theory | Lex Fridman Podcast #12

body.input: And yes, if you have the wrong objective, the AI will optimize that to the hilt. And it's going to

body.input: And now here's my conversation with Steven Pressfield.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Modern society in many ways dreams

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: of creating universal peace.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And yet war has molded civilization

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: as we know it throughout its history.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: So let's start at the high philosophical level.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: If you could imagine a world without war,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: how would that world be different?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Perhaps put another way, what purpose has war served?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Why do we fight?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I think we're basically the same creatures internally

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: that we were in the cave, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: In tribal society, back for however many, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: hundreds of thousands, millions of years,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: which means that we're in the dynamic in our mind

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: is a kind of an us versus them dynamic

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: where our tribe is the people

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: and everybody else or whatever, you know?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And I don't see that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I don't think that's changed one iota over the centuries.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: It's just a question of how one might sublimate

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: that urge to compete.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I mean, you're a martial artist, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: a great part of your day I'm sure is dedicated

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: to reaching that place of, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: of total commitment in the face of competition,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: in the face of adversity, et cetera, et cetera,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: which is I think natural and great for the human race

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: on an individual basis.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: So the hope that I have, if there is any hope,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: personally, I don't think the human race

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: is gonna be around very long,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: but would be in sports

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: or in other kind of sublimated activities

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: where people can act out their need for conquest

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: or aggression or so forth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: but at the same time relate to their opponents

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: as human beings that when the game is over,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: you know, you embrace your competitor and stuff like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: So you think war was inevitable.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: It's a part of human nature as opposed to a force,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: a creative force in society that served a benefit.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Well, I'm sure it has benefited, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: spreading cultures and mixing cultures and stuff like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: But I think the urge to conquest,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: if you think about Alexander the Great or Julius Caesar

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: or Napoleon or anybody like that,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: or even individual, or if we even think about

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: one of the plants that we're looking at right outside,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I mean, if you let a particular plant have its way,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: it would take over, you know, the whole hillside.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And certainly in the days of Alexander the Great, let's say,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: there were, who knows over the face of the earth,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: hundreds of little kingdoms, China, Japan, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Asia, Europe, wherever, and every prince that grew up

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: dreamt of conquering his neighbor

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: and conquering a neighbor after that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: That seems to be a universal human imperative,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: at least in the male of the species.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: So-

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: War is just a realization of that imperative.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I think so.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: So you've written about Spartans in the Battle of Thermopylae,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: you've about Alexander the Great,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: about the Six Day War in 67 in Israel

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: against Egypt, Jordan, Syria.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: What war, not just out of those, but in general,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: do you think has been most transformative for the world?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Well, these are great questions, Lex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Tough, easy ones, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I mean, I wish I knew more about the Mongols,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: because I certainly, from what little I know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I think that was a very, their conquests

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: was a very transformative bringing cultures, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: in a horrible, bloody way together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: But gosh, what's then the most transformative?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Maybe the Roman conquest, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: establishing the Roman Empire and bringing that culture.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Maybe Alexander the Great's wars that, you know,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: united East and West at least for a minute.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: So building of empire.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Do you have a sense, so there's wars,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: I mean, the Six Day War is not about building empires.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: It's about deeply held religious, cultural conflict

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: and holding the line, holding the border.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And then there is conquests, like the Mongols,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: that what is it, some large percentage of the population

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: is a descendant of Genghis Khan, I believe, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: So that has transformative effects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And then World War II, I mean, personally,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: and my family and so on, the transformative effects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Let me ask you this, Lex, why are you,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: what are you trying to get at with these questions?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: What is this kind of the theme that you're aiming at?

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Well, I talked to Eric Weisstein,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: and he said everything is great about war

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: except the killing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And there's a romantic notion of war.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Certainly there's a romantic notion of being a warrior,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: but there's a romantic notion of war

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: that somehow there's a creative force to it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: That because we fight out of that fighting comes culture,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: comes music and art and more and more desire to create

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: with the societies that win.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And to me, war is not just, hey, I have a stick

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: and I want your land.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: It's some kind of, like it has echoes of the creative force

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: that makes humans unique to other animals.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: Like war is, it can't be just four people or 10 people

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: or 100 people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: You have to have thousands of people agreeing,

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: usually thousands or more, for something so deeply

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: that you would be willing to risk your own life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And there's a romantic notion to that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Steven Pressfield: The War of Art | Lex Fridman Podcast #102

body.input: And because you've written so well and passionately
